claims.text: In refractory high-entropy alloys at high temperature, heterogeneous lattice distortion controls the activation of unusual dislocation processes.
The unusual dislocation processes associated with heterogeneous lattice strain include multiple kinks or jogs and bidirectional cross slips.
These unusual dislocation processes mediate alloy strengthening.
These unusual dislocation processes also mediate thermoelastic behavior.
TiZrHfNbMo0.1 is a refractory high-entropy alloy that has been investigated using irradiation and nanoindentation experiments.
The proposed baseline has typical lattice distortion arising from a near-equiatomic distribution of refractory elements.
Adding or reducing minor alloying elements can systematically change lattice mismatch and therefore lattice distortion.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can alter defect density and thereby change lattice distortion.
At temperatures of at least 1000 °C, diffusion is activated in the proposed alloys.
Some refractory high-entropy alloys retain high strength at temperatures of at least 1000 °C.
The proposed alloys remain in a distorted solid-solution regime during the specified high-temperature tests.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases local stress heterogeneity.
Lattice-strain heterogeneity triggers multiple kinks or jogs and bidirectional cross slips.
Altered dislocation activity changes elastic modulus and strain-hardening behavior.
Increasing lattice distortion will increase high-temperature yield strength relative to the baseline.
Increasing lattice distortion will produce a higher elastic modulus relative to the baseline.
Increasing lattice distortion will change the indentation-size-effect profile relative to the baseline.
In irradiated TiZrHfNbMo0.1, increasing irradiation dose produces higher defect density and more serious lattice distortion that limits expansion of the indentation plastic zone.
Oxidation behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys depends strongly on alloy composition and testing conditions.
